scenarios.description: A freight-forwarding platform models customer orders for multi-leg shipments. The OrderService is a Java (Spring Boot) module that records booking confirmations, container assignments and customs clearances. Business rules require that an order line can never be removed once a container has been assigned, that totals are recomputed whenever a leg changes, and that the lifecycle draft -> booked -> in-transit -> delivered -> closed rejects every illegal transition. Auditors replay 90 days of transitions from the event log. Today the order data lives in flat DTO maps shared by the pricing, planning and invoicing modules, so the rules leak into every caller and two modules disagree about what 'booked' means. The decision to implement: how to give one identifiable thing, with stable identity, an explicit lifecycle and enforced invariants, authority over its own state changes.
scenarios.decision_statement: Give the order one identity-bearing owner that enforces its lifecycle transitions and invariants so callers cannot bypass the rules.
scenarios.notes: Sibling set keeps near misses (aggregate vs entity) in play; the description names no pattern term.

scenarios.family: Values, types and correctness by construction
scenarios.description: A treasury service keeps multi-currency account balances for 14 currencies. Amounts arrive as raw BigDecimal together with a currency code string, and every call site decides for itself how to round, whether to allow negative balances and how to compare two amounts. Two production incidents traced back to a debit applied in the wrong currency after a missed null check, and a rounding rule changed in one module without the others following. The accounting team requires that an amount can never exist without its currency, that arithmetic between different currencies is a compile-time or construction-time error rather than a runtime surprise, and that the rounding policy lives in exactly one place. The decision to implement: how to represent the amount-plus-currency pair so illegal combinations cannot be constructed and all arithmetic in the ledger goes through one authoritative representation.
scenarios.decision_statement: Represent an amount together with its currency as one self-validating concept whose operations reject invalid combinations.
scenarios.notes: Holds when a reviewer replaces kotlin: type-object appears for the rounding-policy axis.

scenarios.description: A regulatory reporting service generates quarterly disclosure documents. A report is assembled from a mandatory header and summary, plus an arbitrary combination of optional sections: per-entity tables, footnotes, risk annexes and audit trails. Sections depend on the reporting regime, so the same report is produced in several shapes. The current constructor takes 19 positional arguments, half of them optional booleans, and callers regularly pass them in the wrong order; two teams worked around it by copying a private helper and now the validation rules differ. The finance team wants to compose a report step by step, validate at the end that all mandatory sections are present, and reuse the same assembly recipe for a variant. The decision to implement: how to construct these complex documents step by step, with named steps and a single validation point, without a 19-argument constructor.
scenarios.decision_statement: Assemble the report through explicit named steps that validate completeness before the document is handed out.
scenarios.notes: parameter-object and fluent-interface are the two acceptable supporting axes (data clump + readability).

scenarios.description: A logistics marketplace prices shipments differently per tenant: some tenants price per kilometre, others by weight brackets, a few by full cost-plus contracts, and two enterprise tenants need a rules engine driven by their own tariff file. The pricing service today is one 600-line method with a switch over the tenant type, plus quarterly patches that keep breaking the other branches. Marketing wants to add a promotional pricing scheme next quarter without touching the existing branches, and support wants to see which algorithm produced an offer. The decision to implement: how to encapsulate each pricing computation behind one common call so the caller picks one at runtime, new schemes can be added without editing existing branches, and each scheme stays independently testable.
scenarios.decision_statement: Encapsulate each interchangeable pricing computation behind one common operation that the caller selects at runtime.
scenarios.notes: template-method stays acceptable because the reviewer may prefer an inheritance-based variation.

scenarios.description: A static analysis tool parses Java-like source into a tree of about 40 node types and runs a growing set of analyses over it: dead-code detection, API-usage checks, complexity metrics and a licence-header scan. Every new analysis currently means editing a central switch over node types, and every new node type means touching all analyses; the last parser change broke two analyses that nobody thought about. The analyses need node-specific behaviour plus the ability to accumulate state while walking, and the team wants new analyses as self-contained units that can be shipped and enabled independently. The decision to implement: how to add operations over a fixed hierarchy of node types without editing the node classes, so new analyses do not require touching existing code and node-specific behaviour stays together.
scenarios.decision_statement: Add node-type-specific operations over a stable tree hierarchy without modifying the node classes themselves.
scenarios.notes: Language switched from rust to java because extensible-visitor is discouraged in rust.

scenarios.description: An insurance backend integrates a third-party billing system over a SOAP-ish HTTP API. Every service class that needs an invoice today builds its own request URL, parses the response XML inline and repeats the same retry and timeout handling; three of them disagree about how a rejected invoice is reported. The vendor ships breaking changes twice a year, and after the last upgrade four call sites had to be found and fixed by hand. The team wants exactly one component that knows the vendor protocol, translates it into the internal invoice model and back, enforces the timeout and retry policy, and is the only place that has to change when the vendor moves. The decision to implement: how one component owns access to an external system and maps between its foreign representation and the internal model.
scenarios.decision_statement: Concentrate access to the external billing system in one component that owns its protocol, mapping and error translation.
scenarios.notes: Service-stub and data-transfer-object are the classic alternatives a reviewer may accept for the same seam.

scenarios.description: An order-management platform consumes a single stream of business events (order created, payment captured, shipment delayed, return requested) from a broker. Today one consumer function loads every message, inspects a type field and chains through if-elif to the right handler; shipment-delay handling was added last month and payment events started going to the return handler after a copy-paste mistake. Different event types need different validation, different downstream systems and different retry policies, and the operations team wants to add a channel for a new event type without editing the dispatch chain. The decision to implement: how to send each incoming event to the handler that owns its kind, decided from the message content, while keeping handlers independent and adding new kinds without editing existing routing.
scenarios.decision_statement: Route each incoming event to the handler that owns its kind based on message content, without editing existing branches.
scenarios.notes: Covered also by the flow-with-detour case; splitter stays acceptable for the multi-handler variant.

scenarios.description: A product-catalog service stores roughly two million articles in PostgreSQL, with read replicas, a Redis view cache and an Elasticsearch index kept in sync. Domain code for pricing and assortment curates article objects, but right now it also contains raw SQL, session handling and cache keys, which is why 30 test doubles still speak SQL. The storage layout changes twice a year (a new read replica, a switch to a document index for the search path) and every change ripples through the domain services. The team wants domain code to ask for articles in domain terms and to keep all persistence knowledge in one place, so the storage technology can be replaced behind a stable interface. The decision to implement: how to mediate between domain objects and the store so clients work in collection-like domain queries instead of SQL.
scenarios.decision_statement: Mediate between domain objects and the store behind a collection-like interface so storage details never reach clients.
scenarios.notes: Identity-map is acceptable supporting evidence for the identity/caching axis.

scenarios.description: A payment orchestration service calls an external card processor for every checkout. During last month's outage the processor answered with 2-second timeouts and 503s for 25 minutes; the orchestrator kept retrying hard, its own worker pool saturated, and the checkout flow for unrelated payment methods went down with it. Operations want the orchestrator to notice that the downstream dependency is unhealthy, stop sending traffic for a cooling-off period, let a small amount of probe traffic through to detect recovery, and otherwise fail fast with a clear error instead of queueing work that cannot succeed. The decision to implement: how to wrap calls to the unreliable dependency so repeated failures stop the traffic before the failure spreads to callers.
scenarios.decision_statement: Wrap calls to the unreliable dependency so consecutive failures suspend traffic and a probe detects recovery.
scenarios.notes: bulkhead/fail-fast are the overloading axes; retry-with-backoff is the near-miss sibling.

scenarios.description: A multi-tenant SaaS exposes 120 REST endpoints over an Express/NestJS stack. Authorization today is hand-written inside each handler: some check a role claim, some check a tenant id, four forgot to check anything and were caught only by a pen test. The security team wants every request to pass the same mandatory checks (valid token, tenant binding, role or scope for the operation) before any handler logic runs, with one place that decides and a machine-readable reason in the logs for every denial. Handlers must not be able to skip the checks by accident, and adding a new endpoint must not require copying them. The decision to implement: how to enforce a uniform authorization decision on every incoming request before the request reaches business logic.
scenarios.decision_statement: Enforce one mandatory authorization decision for every incoming request before handler logic executes.
scenarios.notes: Intercepting-validator is the acceptable alternative when a reviewer prefers validation-flavoured naming.

scenarios.description: A configuration engine keeps its own small expression language for 700 rule files: literals, identifiers, unary and binary operators with precedence and parentheses. The current reader is a 400-line regex chain that fails with 'syntax error near 14' and no position context; a precedence bug shipped to production because nobody could review the chain. The team needs the language to grow (function calls, optional chaining) while keeping error messages precise (offset, expected token) and keeping the grammar readable for reviewers. Hand-rolling the reader is preferred over a parser generator so the build stays dependency-light. The decision to implement: how to read the expression language into a tree with explicit precedence handling and recoverable, position-carrying errors.
scenarios.decision_statement: Read the expression language into a syntax tree with explicit precedence and position-carrying errors.
scenarios.notes: Pratt parser stays acceptable for the precedence-climbing variant the reviewer may prefer.

scenarios.description: A billing application is split into domain services, adapters and infrastructure code, but every service constructs its own collaborators: the invoice service news up a Postgres connection pool and a Stripe client in its constructor. Integration tests cannot replace them without patching module globals, the pool is created three times, and a staging incident happened because one service silently used the production DSN compiled into a helper. The team wants the application entry point to decide which concrete implementations exist, to hand each service what it needs, and to allow tests and the staging profile to supply fakes without touching service code. The decision to implement: how a service receives its collaborators from the outside instead of creating them, so configuration and tests control the concrete choices.
scenarios.decision_statement: Have collaborators supplied from the outside at composition time so configuration and tests control concrete choices.
scenarios.notes: Registry/separated-interface are the near-miss siblings a reviewer may prefer for a service locator style.

scenarios.description: A logistics platform must keep talking to a 12-year-old customs-clearance system whose interface is a class with three overloaded submit methods that return an int status code plus a mutable callback object. The internal domain speaks a clean, typed clearance port. Product wants to migrate to a new clearance provider next year, and the current integration code has vendor-specific ints, string statuses and callback threading spread across 40 classes. The team wants exactly one translation layer that turns domain calls into vendor calls and vendor responses into domain results, so the domain never sees the vendor's types and a second provider can be plugged in later. The decision to implement: how to make the incompatible vendor interface usable by the domain through one dedicated translation component that can be replaced.
scenarios.decision_statement: Translate the incompatible vendor interface into the domain's expected port through one replaceable component.

hints.focus: keep the vendor wire format unchanged while the internal model evolves

scenarios.notes: Holdout family: the description intentionally leans on the vendor-interface mismatch only.

scenarios.description: The back-office application of a ticketing platform renders an operator console as server-side HTML. For each screen the current code path is smeared across routing, an ASP.NET view and three partial classes: request parameters are read in the view, validation happens twice, the workflow service is called from the template, and the redirect target is assembled in the markup. Adding a filter field last sprint broke the export button because nobody knew which layer owned the query state. The team wants per-request handling that receives the parsed request, validates it, calls the workflow, chooses the next view, and puts the view data into a presentation model the template can render without logic. The decision to implement: how one component handles a single request through validation, workflow invocation and view selection.
scenarios.decision_statement: Handle one incoming request end to end: parse, validate, invoke the workflow and select the view.
scenarios.notes: Holdout family: front-controller stays acceptable if the reviewer prefers one shared entry point.

scenarios.description: An insurance policy system stores rich domain objects (policies, coverages, endorsements) in a legacy schema with 30 tables whose column names match neither the class attributes nor the current model version. The persistence code is written per service: each one assembles SQL and pulls column values out of the ResultSet in its own order, so a schema change breaks three services and one loader silently swapped two money columns. The mapping must survive schema changes and model refactors independently, keep the domain classes free of persistence annotations, and make it possible to add a second store (document storage for the archive) later. The decision to implement: how to translate between in-memory domain objects and the relational tables so both sides can evolve independently.
scenarios.decision_statement: Translate between domain objects and relational tables in one layer so model and schema evolve independently.
scenarios.notes: Holdout family: active-record is the acceptable near miss when persistence and domain coincide.

scenarios.description: A mobile sync engine on iOS fetches four kinds of payload (contacts, calendar, documents, settings) concurrently and merges them into one local state. The current implementation launches detached tasks per payload, keeps a mutable dictionary across them with a lock, and leaks two tasks on every logout because nothing waits for them; cancellation after a network drop occasionally leaves half-merged state and a background refresh that keeps running into the next session. The team wants a parent work unit that owns its children: if one fails or the user cancels, every child is cancelled and awaited before the merge is abandoned, and the engine reports one outcome to the caller. The decision to implement: how concurrent child tasks are spawned, awaited and cancelled under one parent scope so lifetimes are bounded and cleanup is deterministic.
scenarios.decision_statement: Spawn, await and cancel concurrent child tasks under one parent scope with deterministic cleanup.
scenarios.notes: Holdout family: fork-join/future-promise stay acceptable for the older API-shaped solutions.

scenarios.description: The order service of a commerce platform has a test suite of 240 tests, of which 90 hit a real PostgreSQL and a staging payment provider. They fail on a developer laptop, take 11 minutes in CI and are flaky at month end. The storage and payment collaborators must be replaced so that tests assert what the service asked for (which payment intent, with which amount, in which order) and can force the error paths (declined card, duplicate submit) deterministically, while a handful of tests should still run against the real integration. The team also wants the replacement to fail loudly when the service calls an unexpected collaborator method. The decision to implement: how to stand in for a collaborator during a test so calls can be programmed, observed and verified without touching the real system.
scenarios.decision_statement: Stand in for collaborators in tests so calls can be programmed, observed and verified without the real system.
scenarios.notes: Holdout family: stub/spy are the near misses; fake is acceptable where behaviour matters more than calls.

scenarios.description: An operations dashboard renders live fleet telemetry: 40 widgets over a WebSocket feed, user-selected filters, drill-down panels and a per-widget refresh cadence. Today each widget component stores its own copy of the filter state in local component state, formats numbers inside the template, and re-renders the whole tree on every tick; two panels disagree after a filter change and the charts flicker under load. The team wants presentation state to live in one place per view, to be derived from the model rather than duplicated, and to be observable so a template can bind to it without formatting or fetching logic. Designers also want the same state shape reused for a future mobile view. The decision to implement: how view state is represented and bound so templates stay declarative and multiple views share one state representation.
scenarios.decision_statement: Represent view state once and bind templates to it declaratively so multiple views share one representation.
scenarios.notes: Holdout family: presentation-model is the acceptable sibling when the reviewer avoids the VM framing.
